labels.rationale: Judicious semicolon joins a closely related default/override pair; textbook acceptable use, not a ban.
Parallel contrastive clauses (rename vs. transfer) are exactly the judicious semicolon use Google allows.
Two closely related instructional clauses; semicolon is judicious, not a rule breach.
Parallel do-X/do-Y instructions; a model case of correctly judicious semicolon use.
Contrasts interactive vs. non-TTY behavior; closely related independent clauses, judicious usage.
Actor (installer) is obvious/generic; passive necessarily keeps 'a rule' as topic subject.
Same pattern: passive keeps the portable item as subject; actor is generic/obvious.
Active stative verb ('includes/carries') keeps 'each exit' as subject and is clearer.
'Verification fails' is active, same subject, shorter, and clearer than 'cannot be satisfied.'
Named actor (the ADR) is right there; an active rewrite is easy and clearer.
'Nothing is installed' rhetorically emphasizes the safety guarantee; passive needed to keep that subject.
'CLI reference' is a fixed cross-reference title convention, not incidental prose word choice.
'CLI agent format' reads as Kiro's own product terminology, not generic author prose.
Plain generic prose; 'command-line output' substitutes cleanly with no meaning loss.
CLI is used as a defined contrast term with TUI, standard acronym pairing in this doc's domain.
Heading uses CLI consistently with the doc's established TUI/CLI terminology pair.
"Latest content" accurately names dynamic sync target, not a stale-prone product claim.
"Can see"/"hidden" are conventional, unambiguous technical idioms for filesystem visibility.
Same sentence mixes "you" and "the user" for the same referent, inconsistent reader address.
"This" summarizes the prior sentence's idea, a standard, recoverable usage, not ambiguous.
"Easy" is a flagged minimizing usability word per Google style word list; regex reliably catches it.
"This page covers" matches the canonical preannouncement pattern Google style bans.
"Detects"/"asks" plainly describe automated prompts, not misleading personification.
"It" in "compound it" has no explicit noun antecedent, only an implied complexity concept.
"Will degrade" predicts an outcome of a later translation step, a valid future-tense use.
Same pattern: predicts a translation-time consequence, not current tool behavior.
Consistently third-person description of general modal behavior, not mixed with "you."
"Just" accurately describes what a registry literally is, not a minimizing usability claim.
